reykjavik: Reykjavik's heating is 100% geothermal—even the sidewalks are warmed by volcanic water!
Locals leave babies outside cafes in strollers—even in freezing winter—to nap in the crisp air.
There are no mosquitoes in Iceland. The unique climate makes it impossible for them to breed.
Elves are taken so seriously that road construction is frequently rerouted to protect their 'homes'.
Reykjavik has fewer daylight hours in December than an average movie runtime—just 4 hours.
tromsø: From late May to July, the sun never sets in Tromsø. Midnight hikes are common!
It has the world's northernmost university, brewery, and botanical garden.
Despite being so far north, the Gulf Stream keeps the ocean here completely ice-free.
The city has an underground network of tunnels—complete with roundabouts—to bypass winter snow.
Winter here means absolute darkness for two whole months, but the northern lights are spectacular.
tallinn: Tallinn runs free public transport for all its registered residents.
Estonians invented Skype here! The country is a globally recognized digital superpower.
A medieval pharmacy in the town square has operated continuously in the same spot since 1422.
You can walk along medieval defensive walls that once sprouted 46 massive guard towers.
Local internet is declared a fundamental human right by the Estonian government.
bergen: Bergen is Europe's rainiest city, averaging 239 days of precipitation every year.
The iconic wooden Bryggen wharf buildings notoriously lean sideways due to centuries of settling.
Locals hike up the seven mountains surrounding the city just for fun on weekends.
It was Norway's capital in the 13th century before Oslo claimed the title.
Grieg, the composer of 'In the Hall of the Mountain King', lived and worked here.
helsinki: Finns drink more coffee per capita than anyone else on Earth—nearly 12 kg annually!
Helsinki sits on an archipelago of over 300 islands connected by ferries and bridges.
There are roughly 2 million saunas in Finland; even Helsinki’s Burger King has one.
The city uses a massive underground lake to cool its buildings during the summer.
Helsinki has an official 'Day of Failure' every October to celebrate learning from mistakes.
prague: The Astronomical Clock in Prague is the oldest working clock of its kind, ticking since 1410.
Prague Castle is the largest ancient castle complex in the world, spanning over 70,000 square meters.
One street here is so incredibly narrow it has pedestrian traffic lights to prevent jams.
Beer is literally cheaper than bottled water in many traditional Czech pubs.
The famously winding Vltava River is crossed by 18 majestic bridges.
santorini: Santorini's white-washed towns sit on the rim of an active, submerged volcano caldera.
Vines here are grown in low baskets on the ground to survive fierce Mediterranean winds.
The colorful beaches come in distinct shades of volcanic red, white, and jet black.
Before a massive 1600 BC eruption, the island was circular; now it’s shaped like a croissant.
There are more churches on Santorini than residential houses, mostly tiny family chapels.
istanbul: Istanbul spans two continents! You can have breakfast in Europe and lunch in Asia.
The Grand Bazaar features 61 covered streets and over 4,000 wildly colorful shops.
Tulips originated here, not in Holland! The Ottomans exported them to Europe in the 1500s.
Agatha Christie wrote 'Murder on the Orient Express' in Room 411 of the Pera Palace Hotel.
Hundreds of thousands of beloved stray cats roam the city, cared for collectively by residents.
amsterdam: Amsterdam has precisely 165 canals, collectively stretching over 100 kilometers long.
There are significantly more bicycles in the city than actual residents.
Many narrow canal houses slant forward intentionally so furniture can be hoisted through windows.
The city sits entirely below sea level, kept dry by an intricate system of dykes.
The famous floating flower market has been selling blooms on the Singel canal since 1862.
vienna: Vienna is the only true capital city with massive commercial vineyards flourishing within its limits.
The famous Lipizzaner horses are born dark brown and naturally turn snow white as they age.
Vienna’s Central Cemetery has three million 'residents'—including Beethoven and Schubert.
The oldest continuously operating zoo in the world is located in the gardens of Schönbrunn Palace.
The snow globe was accidentally invented here in 1900 by a mechanic trying to improve lightbulbs.
paris: The Eiffel Tower shrinks during winter! Cold weather makes the iron structure up to 6 inches shorter.
There are exactly 38 true 'bridges' stretching across the Seine river within the city.
Paris has an underground network of catacombs housing the bones of over six million people.
It’s known as the 'City of Light' because it was heavily illuminated to deter 17th-century street crime.
The Louvre is so massive it would take 100 days to see every piece for 30 seconds.
